prompt: A maintenance console schedules either a battery inspection or a battery swap. Both workflows read battery identity, but only the swap may change the aircraft assignment. The inspection client must not receive an assignment-change capability, and neither workflow may write storage fields directly. The storage adapter may change without changing either workflow. What should the public seam expose?

options.text: Give inspection an identity-only reader and give swap that reader plus an assignment-change operation; keep storage fields private.
Give both workflows one maintenance interface with inspect and replace-assignment methods, then hide the swap button in the inspection UI.
Return a mutable BatteryRecord to both clients and rely on each workflow not to change aircraftId during inspection.
Inject FleetBatteryStore into both workflows and let each call its storage methods directly.

feedback.reason: The clients have different allowed operations, so the inspection contract must omit reassignment while the swap contract includes it; both can remain independent of storage representation.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Separate client-facing capabilities make the allowed operation set visible in each contract instead of relying on UI conventions or record-field discipline.
details.scenarioApplication: Inspection receives identity access only. The swap workflow additionally receives the operation that changes aircraft assignment, while both use an implementation that owns storage.
details.errorCorrection: Giving the shared replace method to inspection leaves the forbidden operation callable. A mutable record relies on callers not writing the field, and direct store access couples workflows to the replaceable storage adapter.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A shared capability is suitable only when all clients need the same authority; here the prompt gives inspection and swap different operation sets.
details.transfer: For another pair of clients, compare the operations each is allowed to perform and expose only the corresponding capability to each.

messages.text: The inspection client still receives a callable assignment-change method; hiding its button does not remove that capability.
A mutable record makes assignment changes available to inspection callers and relies on convention instead of the stated boundary.
The storage adapter may change independently, so making both workflows call its concrete storage methods couples them to that representation.

prompt: A referral desk sends referral details to a dispatch boundary. Only that boundary may read the consent ledger, check that consent is active, and build the specialist-facing summary; the desk must not read consent state or construct the summary. The specialist receives the summary, never the internal ledger. A separate audit screen can inspect consent history but cannot dispatch. Which interface boundary fits these clients?

options.text: Give dispatch a consent-checked submit operation and give audit a read-only consent-history view.
Expose the full Referral object, including its consent records, to both clients.
Let the desk read consent state and build the outgoing summary itself.
Create a single administrative API with submit, edit-consent, and inspect-history methods for both clients.

feedback.reason: Dispatch must enforce the consent condition and emit only the summary, while audit needs history without dispatch authority. Separate contracts express both boundaries directly.

details.mechanismOrProperty: An interface can hide sensitive representation while exposing only the operation and result a client needs. The dispatch contract owns the consent check; the audit contract grants observation only.
details.scenarioApplication: The specialist path receives a summary after the active-consent check. The audit client can read history but cannot use that capability to send a referral.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: The specialist-facing client would receive internal consent history that the prompt excludes, and both clients could become coupled to its representation. The desk is expressly not allowed to read consent or construct the summary; that work belongs at the dispatch boundary. The desk and audit screen receive powers they do not need, while the intended separation between disclosure and audit becomes a convention.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A shared broad API is simpler only when clients share authority and data needs; these clients explicitly do not.
details.transfer: Design each boundary around the caller’s permitted operation and output, rather than exporting an aggregate object.

messages.text: The specialist-facing client would receive internal consent history that the prompt excludes, and both clients could become coupled to its representation.
The prompt reserves ledger access and summary construction to the dispatch boundary, not the desk client.
The desk and audit screen receive powers they do not need, while the intended separation between disclosure and audit becomes a convention.

prompt: Each completed practice attempt must retain the exact exercise revision and scoring-policy version used at submission. A history screen reads those recorded values; a scoring service computes a result but must not edit completed attempts. Which contract should callers use?

options.text: Accept an immutable completion command and return a result; expose completed attempt data through a read-only history view.
Give the history screen the attempt object so it can repair version and score fields when policy changes.
Let the scoring service write directly into the attempt’s internal fields.
Publish one PracticeAttempt interface with submit, rescore, rewriteRevision, and editPolicy for every client.

feedback.reason: Submission should capture the versions once, and later readers should observe them without write access. An immutable command/result boundary keeps scoring separate from historical storage.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A contract can separate command inputs from a read-only projection. That prevents a result calculator from acquiring permission to rewrite a completed record.
details.scenarioApplication: The scoring service receives the attempt’s pinned revision and policy and returns the result; history displays the captured values.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: That lets a reader rewrite the historical inputs that the prompt says each completed attempt must retain. The scorer becomes coupled to mutable representation and can change the recorded revision or policy instead of returning a result under the supplied snapshot. It grants history readers and scorers mutation operations that their stated roles do not need, weakening the completed-attempt boundary.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A rescore operation could be added as a separately specified workflow, but this prompt says completed records retain their original scoring inputs.
details.transfer: Use separate command and query contracts when one client creates a record and another must only inspect it.

messages.text: That lets a reader rewrite the historical inputs that the prompt says each completed attempt must retain.
The scorer becomes coupled to mutable representation and can change the recorded revision or policy instead of returning a result under the supplied snapshot.
It grants history readers and scorers mutation operations that their stated roles do not need, weakening the completed-attempt boundary.

prompt: A procurement exception can be prepared by an assistant, but only the named manager may approve it after required controls pass. The queue screen may show status and approver identity; it must not set either directly. Which public contract should the queue call?

options.text: Provide prepare and approve operations that validate the actor and controls, with status exposed as read-only data.
Expose status and approver fields so the queue can mark the exception Approved after checking its own checklist.
Give every queue user prepare, approve, overrideControls, and editApprover operations.
Make the queue depend on a stored-procedure name and table layout rather than an approval operation.

feedback.reason: Preparation and approval are different capabilities. The approve operation can check the named actor and controls, while callers read status without assigning it.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A behavior-focused interface names the authorized transition and hides the stored status representation. This keeps the approval condition at the operation boundary.
details.scenarioApplication: The assistant can prepare; the manager invokes approval; the queue reads the resulting status and approver identity.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: The queue is not the authorized decision point in the stated workflow; direct field writes can record approval without the named manager operation. The contract grants assistants the exact approval and override powers the prompt reserves to the named manager after controls pass. That exposes storage/procedure details instead of the stable action and conditions that callers need; a representation change would ripple into the queue.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A caller-side checklist alone would be sufficient only if every caller were trusted to enforce the approval rule, which the prompt denies.
details.transfer: Represent authority boundaries as distinct contract operations, not editable status fields.

messages.text: The queue is not the authorized decision point in the stated workflow; direct field writes can record approval without the named manager operation.
The contract grants assistants the exact approval and override powers the prompt reserves to the named manager after controls pass.
That exposes storage/procedure details instead of the stable action and conditions that callers need; a representation change would ripple into the queue.

prompt: The venue-pass registry stores a PassRow with an internal row number and database column names. Kiosk and mobile clients need only the durable pass ID, displayed zone, and expiration time; the database row layout will change, and clients must not read or update persistence fields. What should the lookup contract expose?

options.text: Return a PassSummary value with pass ID, displayed zone, and expiration; keep row keys and persistence fields inside the registry.
Return PassRow directly and document its current column names as the client contract.
Return a dictionary keyed by the current database column names so clients can select the fields they need.
Give each client the concrete SQL repository so it can query the row fields it needs.

feedback.reason: A small public projection preserves the client’s required pass data while allowing the registry to change its row representation independently.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A public value projection defines the data the caller may depend on without making storage columns part of the API.
details.scenarioApplication: The clients receive pass ID, displayed zone, and expiry; the registry retains its internal row number and database layout.
details.errorCorrection: Returning PassRow or a column-keyed dictionary makes the current persistence shape observable to clients. Giving them the repository also exposes the storage boundary and lets each client depend on implementation details.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Expose a persistence entity only when its fields are intentionally part of the caller contract; this scenario explicitly excludes them.
details.transfer: When storage can change independently, identify the stable caller data and return that projection instead of the persistence record.

messages.text: Documenting current column names does not make them stable; the prompt says the row layout will change and is outside the client contract.
The dictionary still exposes database column names, so a row-layout change forces client changes.
Direct repository access makes each client depend on the storage implementation whose layout is changing.

prompt: A temporary role grant has a fixed expiry and an approval reference. A reviewer can approve or reject; a resource screen only needs to know whether the grant currently permits access. The resource screen must not extend or edit grants. Which contract should it depend on?

options.text: A read-only access query that answers whether the grant is effective at a supplied instant.
Give the resource screen grant creation, approval, rejection, and expiry-edit methods.
Expose the expiry timestamp and let the resource screen extend it when access is denied.
Return a mutable permission map that callers can edit for temporary access.

feedback.reason: The resource screen needs a decision, not grant-management authority or the fields used to derive it. A query operation preserves that narrow dependency.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Information hiding lets the grant own the meaning of “effective” while a caller sees only the answer it needs.
details.scenarioApplication: The resource screen supplies the instant and receives an access decision. Reviewer workflows keep their separate state-changing operations.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: Those are reviewer/admin powers, while the resource screen is expressly a consumer that only asks whether access is permitted. The screen is also forbidden to extend the fixed expiry, and a mutable permission map would let callers bypass the grant’s approval and expiry.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The screen may display the expiry value, but it needs the grant’s read-only access decision and cannot use expiry data to extend the grant.
details.transfer: Let the owner interpret its state and expose a read-only query when clients need a decision rather than representation.

messages.text: Those are reviewer/admin powers, while the resource screen is expressly a consumer that only asks whether access is permitted.
The screen is expressly forbidden to extend grants; exposing the expiry does not authorize it to change one.
Caller edits could bypass the grant’s approval and fixed expiry instead of asking the grant contract for its current effective state.

prompt: A notary seals the exact immutable document revision whose digest the signer confirmed. The signing screen may request sealing and display the result; it must not choose a digest by reading revision storage. What should the contract require?

options.text: A seal operation takes the confirmed revision identity and digest, then returns sealed or a digest-mismatch result.
Expose document bytes to the screen and let it calculate and persist the seal digest.
Offer sealCurrent() with no revision input and let the signer confirm afterward.
Allow the screen to replace revision content after sealing while keeping the same seal record.

feedback.reason: The operation must bind the signer’s confirmation to a specific immutable revision and report mismatch without sealing. The caller should not manipulate revision bytes or storage.

details.mechanismOrProperty: An explicit contract input makes the reviewed identity part of the operation’s observable guarantee; private storage remains hidden.
details.scenarioApplication: The signer supplies the revision identity and confirmed digest; the owner checks them and returns the outcome.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: The screen would own the representation and persistence details; the prompt makes the revision owner responsible for checking the signer’s exact confirmation. The operation can seal a different current revision from the one the signer confirmed, which defeats the stated exact-revision contract. That breaks the link between the seal and the immutable revision whose digest was confirmed.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A no-argument “seal current” API would be sufficient only if the current revision were guaranteed to be the exact confirmed one, which is not stated.
details.transfer: Pass the identity that establishes the caller’s intent into the operation that enforces it.

messages.text: The screen would own the representation and persistence details; the prompt makes the revision owner responsible for checking the signer’s exact confirmation.
The operation can seal a different current revision from the one the signer confirmed, which defeats the stated exact-revision contract.
That breaks the link between the seal and the immutable revision whose digest was confirmed.

prompt: A payout status screen receives updates after a separate settlement service initiates transfers. Reconciliation staff may look up a known request ID and must distinguish Pending, Released with its reference, and Rejected; the screen must never initiate or retry a transfer. Which result contract preserves those distinct outcomes?

options.text: Return a typed status result with Pending, Rejected, or Released(payoutReference) from a read-only lookup by request ID.
Give it the full payout service, including Release and GetStatus, so one client can both inspect and initiate transfers.
Expose only IsReleased(requestId) and make the screen infer Pending or Rejected from a false result.
Return the mutable payout ledger record and let the screen update its status after inspecting it.

feedback.reason: The lookup must preserve three distinct states and the released reference; a typed result carries those differences without adding a transfer command.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A tagged status result keeps the possible outcomes distinct and attaches the payout reference only to the Released case.
details.scenarioApplication: The reconciliation screen queries by request ID and receives Pending, Rejected, or Released with its reference, while the separate settlement service retains transfer authority.
details.errorCorrection: A boolean merges Pending and Rejected and loses the release reference. A mutable ledger record makes an observer a writer, while the full payout service gives the screen a transfer command it is forbidden to use.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A single boolean is enough only when the caller needs one yes/no distinction; this screen needs three states and a payload for one of them.
details.transfer: When a caller must distinguish several outcomes, use a result shape that preserves each outcome and its case-specific data.

messages.text: The full service includes Release, even though this screen is limited to observing transfer outcomes.
False cannot distinguish Pending from Rejected and does not provide the reference for a Released payout.
A mutable ledger record lets the display client change the status it should only observe.

prompt: A transit board stores notices with effective instants and sequence numbers. Passenger displays need the currently applicable platform and the next scheduled change; only the controller may append a correction. Which interface best limits client coupling?

options.text: Expose query methods for current and next platform, plus an append-correction command for the controller.
Give every display the mutable ordered notice collection and have each choose the current platform.
Expose setPlatform(code) and let the controller overwrite the platform field.
Publish the board’s table schema and require each client to issue custom queries.

feedback.reason: Passenger displays need derived answers, while the controller alone appends corrections. Query and command operations communicate those distinct needs without exposing the notice collection.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A stable abstraction lets the owner interpret effective ordering and preserves the correction history internally.
details.scenarioApplication: Displays ask for the current or next platform. The controller submits a correction through the operation that can retain ordering data.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: Every display would implement its own effective-time ordering, and the prompt reserves correction writes to the controller. A direct value write loses the effective instant and sequence history that the passenger displays use to determine what applies. Clients become coupled to storage layout even though the public need is two stable queries and one controlled correction operation.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Returning the raw notices is useful for an authorized audit client, but it is unnecessary for passenger rendering and exposes more state than required.
details.transfer: Give each client the result it needs, and reserve mutation operations for the client with that responsibility.

messages.text: Every display would implement its own effective-time ordering, and the prompt reserves correction writes to the controller.
A direct value write loses the effective instant and sequence history that the passenger displays use to determine what applies.
Clients become coupled to storage layout even though the public need is two stable queries and one controlled correction operation.

prompt: Every deployed ArchiveReader can open a document by ID. Only some providers maintain a full-text index; others are legacy plugins that cannot be changed or rebuilt for this release. The search screen must offer search only when the selected provider supports it, and the reader adapter alone can access each provider’s index. Which contract lets new indexed providers add search without changing the base reader or pretending legacy providers can search?

options.text: Keep ArchiveReader.open(id) as the base contract and let indexed providers separately implement SearchableArchive.search(query); the screen offers search only when that capability is present.
Add search(query) to ArchiveReader and require every legacy provider to return an empty result when it has no index.
Have the screen inspect each provider name and call its private index API when that provider is on a hard-coded list.
Have the screen download every document through open(id) and run full-text search locally for all providers.

feedback.reason: Search is not supported by every existing reader, so it belongs in a separate capability that only indexed providers advertise. The base read contract stays usable by unchanged legacy plugins.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A separate capability interface represents an operation available from only some implementations without widening the required method set of the base interface.
details.scenarioApplication: All providers continue to satisfy ArchiveReader.open. Indexed providers also satisfy SearchableArchive, which the screen checks before presenting the search action.
details.errorCorrection: The required base method forces unchanged legacy providers to acquire a search contract they cannot fulfill; a fake empty result is not the same as an unsupported capability. Provider-name branches leak private index APIs into the screen, and downloading every document contradicts the stated boundary that only the adapter can access provider indexes.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A uniform search method would fit if every reader could meet the same search contract, but the prompt explicitly says existing readers cannot all do so.
details.transfer: When only some implementations support an operation, keep the common contract valid for all and expose the extra behavior as an explicit capability.

messages.text: This adds a required operation that unchanged legacy readers cannot provide; an empty result would falsely represent a search with no matches.
The screen becomes coupled to provider names and private index APIs instead of asking the selected reader for a supported capability.
The prompt reserves index access to the reader adapter, and transferring all documents to the screen crosses that boundary.

prompt: A caption stream can use Provider A or Provider B. Both accept a caption chunk and return text plus the chunk’s source timestamp; provider startup errors have a shared error category. The studio may switch providers without changing stream callers. What seam should it define?

options.text: A CaptionProvider contract with the common chunk input, timestamped result, and normalized startup/error outcome.
Make CaptionStudio branch on provider names and call each provider’s distinct methods directly.
Expose each provider’s endpoint, language fields, and internal client object to CaptionStudio callers.
Keep Provider A’s concrete class as the stream contract and wrap Provider B only at the UI.

feedback.reason: Both providers already meet the same input, output, and error shape, so a shared contract allows the stream to use either without provider-specific branches.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Dynamic interchangeability begins with an explicit common interface boundary. Here the contract is warranted by the observed common chunk/result behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: The supervisor selects a provider implementation; stream clients continue using the same chunk call and receiving the same timestamped result form.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: Adding a provider then changes the studio’s dispatch code, despite the prompt stating that both providers already share the same caller-visible behavior. Callers would depend on provider representation instead of the common chunk/result/error contract. That leaves non-UI stream clients tied to one implementation and does not create the common seam the scenario needs.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An adapter is still needed if a provider cannot meet the common contract; this case states both can.
details.transfer: When multiple implementations already share observable behavior, define their common caller-facing contract.

messages.text: Adding a provider then changes the studio’s dispatch code, despite the prompt stating that both providers already share the same caller-visible behavior.
Callers would depend on provider representation instead of the common chunk/result/error contract.
That leaves non-UI stream clients tied to one implementation and does not create the common seam the scenario needs.

prompt: A volunteer swap command receives two assignment IDs. The roster UI needs an outcome and, on rejection, the specific assignment that became unavailable. It should not fetch and rewrite each assignment separately because both must change together. Which boundary is best?

options.text: Offer one SwapAssignments(firstId, secondId) operation that returns Swapped or Rejected with the assignment that blocked the pair.
Let the UI update the first assignment, then the second, and compensate the first if the second update fails.
Give the UI a roster snapshot and a canSwap check, then let it write both assignment fields itself.
Return only a rejection boolean and require the UI to inspect every assignment to discover the blocker.

feedback.reason: The swap is one joint operation, and the UI needs the particular assignment that prevented it; one boundary can own the pair and return that result.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A contract can make an atomic domain action explicit and return enough failure detail without exposing the roster’s internal collections.
details.scenarioApplication: The UI submits both assignment IDs once. The roster owner either applies the pair or reports which assignment blocked it, without exposing its mutable roster.
details.errorCorrection: Sequential writes can expose a partial swap before compensation. A snapshot/check still leaves the UI responsible for both writes and the joint rule. A boolean omits the blocking assignment the prompt requires the UI to identify.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separate writes are appropriate only when intermediate states are allowed; the prompt requires the two assignments to change together.
details.transfer: When a caller needs a multi-record change to succeed or fail as one action, expose that action and its useful failure detail rather than the mutable records.

messages.text: The first update may be visible before the second fails; compensating afterward still exposes a partial-swap interval.
The UI would perform both writes and enforce the joint rule instead of submitting one swap operation to the roster owner.
A boolean does not identify the assignment the UI must show as the blocker.

prompt: Offline route edits contain a parent revision ID and proposed geometry. The editor must receive a conflict containing both revision IDs when accepted geometry changed; no caller may overwrite the current route directly. What should the route boundary expose?

options.text: A submitEdit operation returning accepted or conflict with the current and proposed revision IDs.
Expose the current geometry and let the editor replace it after comparing shapes.
Return only “merge failed” when a conflict occurs.
Make every editor depend on the route file format and write a replacement file.

feedback.reason: The route owner must decide whether the parent revision is still current and return both identities on conflict. The caller should submit intent, not replace geometry storage.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A revision-aware operation hides representation while making stale-write outcomes part of the public contract.
details.scenarioApplication: The editor submits a proposal against its parent revision; it receives acceptance or the exact competing revisions.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: That makes the editor responsible for conflict detection and permits a stale edit to overwrite accepted geometry. The editor cannot identify the two revisions involved, which are required in the stated conflict result. This couples callers to serialization details and bypasses the route owner’s revision check.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A geometry-level merge can be offered separately, but the prompt requires explicit conflict reporting rather than silent automatic resolution.
details.transfer: Expose concurrency outcomes as part of the contract and keep stored representation behind the owner.

messages.text: That makes the editor responsible for conflict detection and permits a stale edit to overwrite accepted geometry.
The editor cannot identify the two revisions involved, which are required in the stated conflict result.
This couples callers to serialization details and bypasses the route owner’s revision check.

prompt: A campaign host applies rewards under a selected ruleset revision. The character page may request a claim and show eligibility, but must not change quest completion; the evaluator can read current legal campaign state. Which interface should the page use?

options.text: A claim operation keyed by character and ruleset revision that returns eligibility/result without editing quest state.
Expose quest completion flags so the page can mark a qualifying quest complete before claiming.
Copy reward rules into the character page and calculate eligibility there.
Expose a universal mutable Character object with methods for quests, rewards, and rulesets to every caller.

feedback.reason: The page needs to request a claim and display its result; the evaluator owns interpretation of current campaign state. The contract also prevents the claim path from editing quest completion.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A purpose-specific operation hides rule storage and separates the caller’s request from the owner’s state evaluation.
details.scenarioApplication: The page supplies the selected ruleset revision and character identity, then renders the returned eligibility or claim result.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: That lets the page manufacture the prerequisite the prompt explicitly says the reward operation must not change. The page would be coupled to ruleset representation and could apply a different revision from the selected campaign rules. The page receives quest-state mutation authority and the evaluator’s role is no longer separated from display and claim requests.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A read-only eligibility query may be useful for previews, but it must not be mistaken for a claim or given quest mutation powers.
details.transfer: Separate request, evaluation, and unrelated state mutation in the public contract.

messages.text: That lets the page manufacture the prerequisite the prompt explicitly says the reward operation must not change.
The page would be coupled to ruleset representation and could apply a different revision from the selected campaign rules.
The page receives quest-state mutation authority and the evaluator’s role is no longer separated from display and claim requests.

prompt: A dispatcher may propose a carrier for a shipment. The carrier must acknowledge custody and satisfy the shipment’s temperature band; a new carrier is not assigned until both checks pass. On rejection, the dispatcher must tell the carrier whether acknowledgment or the temperature band blocked the handoff before resubmission. A tracking screen only reads current custody. What API boundary fits?

options.text: A handoff operation taking a carrier proposal and returning accepted or a typed acknowledgement/band failure; expose custody read-only.
Let the dispatcher assign carrierId first, then ask the carrier adapter whether it can comply.
Expose mutable shipment carrier and temperature fields to the tracking screen.
Return accepted/rejected without identifying which handoff condition failed.

feedback.reason: The handoff is conditional and the tracking screen only observes its result. One command can enforce both conditions and report which one failed.

details.mechanismOrProperty: An operation-focused contract combines the handoff checks with a result detailed enough for the required rejection response, while keeping custody read-only to observers.
details.scenarioApplication: The dispatcher submits a candidate; custody changes only after both conditions pass. A rejection identifies whether acknowledgment or temperature compatibility failed, and tracking reads the committed carrier.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: Assignment becomes visible before the required acknowledgement and temperature check complete. A reader gains write access and can bypass the handoff operation’s two stated conditions. A generic rejection does not tell the dispatcher which condition the carrier must correct before resubmission.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A carrier compatibility query alone is not enough because the prompt also requires acknowledgment before assignment.
details.transfer: When a caller must resolve a rejected conditional change, return the failed condition it needs to address and keep committed state read-only to observers.

messages.text: Assignment becomes visible before the required acknowledgement and temperature check complete.
A reader gains write access and can bypass the handoff operation’s two stated conditions.
A generic rejection omits which condition the dispatcher must tell the carrier to correct.

prompt: A repayment allocation can span several loans, but posted allocations must never reduce any loan below zero. The steward may preview a proposed allocation; only a separate posting action writes ledger entries. Which interface is clearest?

options.text: Expose previewAllocation as a pure result and postAllocation as a validated command; do not expose mutable balances.
Let the steward adjust each loan balance and then record the repayment total.
Use one preview call that also posts the allocation automatically.
Expose the full ledger rows so each caller can calculate and insert allocations.

feedback.reason: Preview and posting have different observable effects, so the interface should name them separately. The posting operation can validate allocations without exposing balance storage.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Explicit command and non-mutating query contracts make side effects visible and hide the ledger representation.
details.scenarioApplication: The steward can inspect the preview before invoking a separate posting operation; only the latter creates allocation entries.
details.errorCorrection: The other options fail for different case-specific reasons: That allows intermediate or inconsistent balances and bypasses the stated no-negative invariant. It violates the prompt’s separation between preview and posting and makes a read-like request unexpectedly mutate the ledger. Callers would depend on storage details and duplicate the allocation invariant instead of using the ledger boundary.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Combining preview and post could be right if every preview is intended to commit, but the prompt explicitly separates them.
details.transfer: Name operations according to their side effects so callers can reason about what a contract may change.

messages.text: That allows intermediate or inconsistent balances and bypasses the stated no-negative invariant.
It violates the prompt’s separation between preview and posting and makes a read-like request unexpectedly mutate the ledger.
Callers would depend on storage details and duplicate the allocation invariant instead of using the ledger boundary.

prompt: A diagram renderer receives an ordered list of CanvasElement objects from installed extensions. Each element type has its own drawing behavior, and new extension types may be installed without editing the renderer. The renderer must preserve the supplied order. Which design lets it draw the mixed list through one stable contract?

options.text: Define CanvasElement.draw(context); iterate the supplied list in order and invoke draw on each element.
Add a renderer switch branch for each extension type and call that type’s drawing routine.
Expose each extension’s shape-specific fields and make the renderer calculate every shape itself.
Group the list by extension type, then invoke one renderer routine per group.

feedback.reason: Each element owns the drawing behavior for its concrete shape, so one polymorphic call handles known and newly installed types. Iterating the original list also preserves its required order.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A common operation can dispatch to each implementation’s behavior while the collection processor depends only on the stable interface.
details.scenarioApplication: The renderer walks the received sequence and calls draw(context) on each CanvasElement; extensions supply their own shape-specific implementation.
details.errorCorrection: A type switch must be edited for new extension kinds, exposing the renderer to every concrete type. Reading shape-specific fields centralizes those differences in the renderer, while grouping changes the supplied drawing order.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Concrete-type handling belongs in the element only because the prompt assigns each extension its own drawing behavior; ordering remains the renderer’s responsibility.
details.transfer: For a heterogeneous collection whose members own variant behavior, call the shared operation polymorphically and keep collection-wide sequencing with the caller.

messages.text: A new extension type would require a renderer branch, contrary to the stated no-renderer-edit extension requirement.
This makes the renderer depend on every shape representation and moves each extension’s drawing behavior into the caller.
Grouping by type can reorder elements, violating the renderer’s supplied-order requirement.

prompt: An archive contains tens of millions of records, so clients must read it in pages. The archive adapter currently uses numeric offsets, but its next storage version will use continuation tokens; the UI must keep requesting pages without learning either storage scheme. What should the public page-reading contract expose?

options.text: Return a page with an opaque continuation handle and accept that handle on the next read; only the archive adapter interprets it.
Expose the database offset and require the UI to add the page size for every next request.
Return all records to the UI once so it can paginate the complete collection locally.
Return each provider’s native continuation syntax and let the UI construct the next provider-specific request.

feedback.reason: An opaque continuation handle lets the UI continue traversal while the adapter changes how it locates the next page. The public contract remains about reading the next page, not about database positioning.

details.mechanismOrProperty: An opaque cursor preserves a stable traversal contract while hiding whether the implementation uses offsets, tokens, or another storage mechanism.
details.scenarioApplication: The UI passes back the continuation handle returned with one page; the archive adapter interprets it and returns the next page and handle.
details.errorCorrection: A numeric offset exposes the current database strategy, downloading the whole archive contradicts the stated scale, and provider-native syntax makes the UI depend on details that vary across adapters.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Offsets are suitable when pagination strategy is intentionally part of the public contract; here a storage migration must not require a UI change.
details.transfer: When a caller needs to continue a traversal but not control its storage position, pass back an opaque continuation value.

messages.text: The UI would depend on the current numeric-offset strategy, which the prompt says will change.
Returning tens of millions of records at once contradicts the required paged access.
Native continuation syntax varies by provider, so exposing it couples the UI to each adapter’s storage protocol.
